html:
On the map for 3000 and 2000 BCE, "city-states" marks the land between the Mediterranean coast and the middle Euphrates, in what is now Syria and the edge of Iraq. Here, as in Sumer to the southeast, people lived in walled cities, each with its own king, gods and farmland.

The best known are Ebla near Aleppo, whose palace archive of thousands of cuneiform tablets was found in the 1970s, and Mari on the Euphrates, a rich trading city with a huge palace. On the coast, Byblos traded cedar wood with Egypt. To the northeast lived the Hurrians.

These cities traded, made treaties and fought each other. Sargon of Akkad and his grandson raided as far as Ebla in the 2300s BCE. Later, Mari was a great power until Hammurabi of Babylon sacked it around 1761 BCE.
